title: Pediatric arrest during dialysis
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: Mika, 6, last reliable dry weight 19 kg (today’s 21 kg reading is questioned), dialyzes through a tunneled catheter. One hour in she is unresponsive and pulseless; a slow wide rhythm became a flat line confirmed in two leads. Compressions have started. The drug nurse asks, “Epinephrine, how much?” Someone reads the ampule: “1 mg per mL.”

n1.prompt: Which path, and when is epinephrine given?

choices.text: Nonshockable (asystole): epinephrine as early as possible.
choices.feedback: PALS 2025: initial epinephrine as early as possible in nonshockable arrest (COR 2a). Then every 3 to 5 minutes; 15:2 with two rescuers.

choices.text: Shock first at 2 J/kg, since a child’s arrest may be a rhythm you cannot see on the screen.
choices.then: The leader moves to the nonshockable path.

choices.text: 19 kg: about 0.2 mg, about 2 mL of 0.1 mg/mL; read aloud and checked.
choices.feedback: Weight, dose, volume and concentration said aloud prevent tenfold errors. 0.01 mg/kg = 0.19 mg (about 0.2 mg per protocol); a second nurse checks.

choices.text: 2 mL from the 1 mg/mL ampule, so the volume is easy to draw up quickly.
choices.feedback: That is 2 mg, ten times her dose.
choices.then: The second nurse catches it: 0.1 mg/mL is used.

choices.text: Use the questioned 21 kg reading, since it is the most recent weight on the chart.
choices.feedback: Use the protocol’s reliable weight or a length-based tape.

n3.scene: The circuit nurse is at the machine. No air, no hemolysis, no reaction signs.

choices.text: Stop fluid removal and the pump; return the blood per protocol; aspirate the lock first.
choices.feedback: Small children: the circuit is a large share of blood volume; lock first. In a 19 kg child (about 1,520 mL blood volume) the circuit blood matters; aspirate the catheter lock before using a limb for drugs.

choices.text: Push epinephrine straight into the catheter limb, since it is the fastest central route available.
choices.feedback: The lock (heparin or citrate) would go in first.
choices.then: The circuit nurse aspirates the lock first.

choices.text: 2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg; compress after each.
choices.feedback: PALS 2025: 2 to 4 J/kg first (2 J/kg for teaching), then 4 J/kg. About 40 J, the nearest setting.

choices.text: 200 J, the adult setting, so the first shock is strong enough to work.
choices.feedback: Pediatric energies are weight-based; 200 J is 10 J/kg for her, the maximum, not the first shock.

end.title: 10:25 a.m.
end.text: After a shock at 2 J/kg and continued CPR, Mika regains a pulse and is transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. The dose card and syringe labels are reviewed at the debrief.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Weight, dose, volume, concentration aloud, with a second check.
  • Arrest epinephrine is 0.1 mg/mL: 0.1 mL/kg.
  • Energies by weight: 2, then 4, up to 10 J/kg or the adult dose.
  • In small children the circuit blood matters; lock before drugs.
